title: Spatial spread of infection: transitions between pulled and pushed fronts
abstract: We consider the spatial spread of epidemic into an unstable, healthy state. When the transmission rate depends on the fraction of infected, the propagating pulse of infection can be either a pulled front or a pushed front. We determined the phase space of parameters for the pulled and pushed regions both by numerically solving the spatial SIR partial differential equations and by a theoretical analysis of the front propagation phenomenon. We found both a continuous and a discontinuous transition between the pulled and pushed front solutions; in the latter transition, the front speed undergoes a jump as a certain parameter crosses the critical threshold. The behavior of the propagating pulses near the transitions has been analyzed and a good agreement between the theory and numerics has been observed. Finally, a bistable region where both pushed and pulled propagating pulses can be realized has been discovered.
summary: This paper analyzes how an epidemic spreads spatially using a modified SIR model, focusing on the transition between 'pulled' and 'pushed' front propagation regimes. The authors use both theory and numerical simulations to map out parameter regions where these transitions occur, revealing continuous jumps, abrupt speed changes, and bistability. This work provides insights into nonlinear pattern formation dynamics applicable across various physical systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how the spatial spread of an infection (epidemic) transitions between two distinct propagation regimes: 'pulled' fronts and 'pushed' fronts.
main_result: The system exhibits both continuous and discontinuous transitions between these front types, and a region of bistability exists where either type of pulse can be realized depending on initial conditions.
method: The research combines theoretical analysis of front propagation with numerical solutions of the spatial Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) partial differential equations.
model_or_system: The model is an SIR epidemiological framework where the transmission rate depends nonlinearly on the fraction of infected individuals. The dynamics are governed by coupled PDEs describing the concentration changes in S, I, and R over space and time.
key_observables: Front speed (c), phase diagram boundaries separating pulled/pushed regimes, and the existence/size of a bistable region.
important_parameters: The minimum transmission rate ($ ar{r}_{\min}$), the parameter $ ar{I}$, and critical thresholds that define transition points.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes propagation into an unstable (healthy) state, and the model is acknowledged as a 'toy model' with unknown exact dependencies for the transmission rate.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase plane showing the border between pulled and pushed regions on $( ar{r}_{\min},  ar{I})$, and provide profiles comparing the shapes of pulled versus pushed front solutions.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the nonlinear SIR model, performing theoretical analysis to characterize front types, numerically solving the PDEs using shooting methods, and finally mapping out the parameter space exhibiting continuous jumps, discontinuous jumps, and bistability.
why_interesting: While applied to epidemiology, the mathematical framework of pattern formation, phase transitions (continuous vs. jump), and bistability in nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems is highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum many-body systems or open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Phase plane of parameters: the border between the regions of pulled and pushed fronts, ¯rmax = 2.8. Black circles are computed from the numerical solution of Eqs. (2-3). Blue squares are computed by employing the “shooting” numerical procedure, see text.

Figure 2 shows an example of the pulled and pushed front proﬁles for both the fraction of infected (Fig. 2a) and the fraction of susceptible (Fig. 2b). As the tran- sition across the border between the pulled and pushed regions can be discontinuous, the pulled and pushed front proﬁles can be remarkably diﬀerent. In the pushed case (black dash-dotted lines), the amplitude of the infection pulse is higher (and therefore the remaining fraction of susceptible is lower) and the pulse decays faster compared to the pulled case (blue solid lines).

FIG. 2: The fraction of infected (a) and the fraction of suscep- tible (b): pulled and pushed front proﬁles. The parameters are ¯rmin = 1.06, ¯rmax = 2.8, ¯I = 0.0800 (pulled front, blue solid line) and ¯I = 0.0745 (pushed front, black dash-dotted line).

FIG. 3: Continuous transition: Front speed as a function of ¯I. The pushed front asymptotics is given by cpushed = cpulled + β(¯Ic −¯I)2, the blue dotted line, see text. The parameters are: ¯rmin = 1.7, ¯rmax = 2.8, β ≃10.714, ¯Ic ≃0.127.

Red circles denote the speeds of the pushed fronts, while black squares denote the speeds of the pulled fronts as computed from the numerical solution of Eqs. (1). The theoretical pulled front speed is shown by the blue solid line.
